text: Jesus didn't say, "Sin no more, and then I won't condemn you." He said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."
explanation:
When her accusers had all slipped away, Jesus asked the woman caught in adultery, "Where are those accusers of yours? Has no one condemned you?" "No one, Lord." The only person present without sin, the one who could have thrown the first stone, said, "Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more."

He didn't excuse her sin; He paid for it, because one day it would be laid on Him at the cross. The church often gets the order backwards. It's the gift of no condemnation that gives you the power to go and sin no more.

text: John 8 opens with a sinner set "in the midst." It ends with Jesus passing "through the midst." Grace takes the centre.
explanation:
The scribes and Pharisees brought the woman and "set her in the midst," a sinner on display, the centre of attention, to trap Jesus. The chapter ends with them picking up stones to throw at Him, and Jesus "going through the midst of them," passing by unseen.

It begins and ends with stones, and it begins with sin in the centre and ends with the Saviour in the centre. Religious minds keep sin at the centre. When Jesus is at the centre of your life, your marriage and your thinking, sin loses its place on the stage.

text: When challenged about the law, Jesus wrote on the ground with His finger: the same finger that wrote the law on stone.
explanation:
The religious leaders thought they had Him cornered. If He said "Stone her," where was His message of grace? If He said "Don't," He was breaking Moses' law. Jesus stooped down and wrote on the ground with His finger, just as the tablets at Sinai were "written with the finger of God." He was the Lawgiver.

Then He stood and said, "He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first," and stooped to write again. One by one, from the oldest to the youngest, they left. The law's light, turned on her accusers, exposed them all.

text: The first sword in the Bible blocked the way back to Eden. The last one fell on the Shepherd, and the way home is open.
explanation:
After the fall, God placed cherubim and "a flaming sword which turned every way" to guard the way to the tree of life. Justice barred sinful man from God's presence, for his own sake.

The last mention of a sword in the Old Testament is "Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd… Strike the Shepherd." Jesus, carrying all our sins, walked into that sword. Judgment found its resting place in His body. Now the voice says, "Come home," and the way in is called "new and living": the nearer you come, the more you live.

text: You can't sweep darkness out of a room. You let the light in.
explanation:
As a boy, one preacher rolled over a boulder by the sea and found a nest of tiny scorpions underneath. He ran off, scared. When he came back, the sun had been shining on that spot, and they were all gone.

Some habits, fears and depressions won't go however hard you fight them. Let the light shine in. David said, "I have more understanding than all my teachers, for Your testimonies are my meditation." They had more knowledge; he had more light. The more of Jesus you see, the less room darkness has.

text: A baby's tears in a basket moved Pharaoh's daughter, and set a nation's deliverance in motion.
explanation:
Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to die. Moses' mother put him in a basket among the reeds, trusting God. Pharaoh's own daughter came down to bathe, opened the basket, "and behold, the baby wept. So she had compassion on him."

Nothing is smaller than a baby's tears, yet God used them to save the boy who would deliver Israel. Years later, God asked Moses, "What is that in your hand?" It was just a shepherd's staff, and it became the rod of God. Never think you're too small for God to use.

text: Jesus did His first miracle not in Jerusalem at a feast, but in tiny Cana, to save an unnamed couple from embarrassment.
explanation:
If Jesus had had a publicist, the first miracle would have been staged in Jerusalem during a great feast, near the temple, before thousands. Instead it was at a village wedding in Cana, still a small town today, where the wine had run out. The bride and groom aren't even named.

He didn't do things for show; He did them to meet needs. The God of eternity laid in a manger, grew up in lowly Nazareth, and turned water into wine for a peasant couple. Can we stoop to serve our own families the same way, and sometimes just bite our lips instead of insisting on being right?
